paragraphs.heading: The biggest eruption on record
paragraphs.text: Mount Tambora is a volcano on Sumbawa, an island in what is now Indonesia. Its eruption in April 1815 is now counted as the most powerful in recorded human history. It scored 7 on the volcanic explosivity index, or VEI, and no confirmed eruption since then has reached that score.

paragraphs.heading: Centuries of quiet
paragraphs.text: Before 1815 the volcano had been dormant for several centuries. That quiet came from magma cooling gradually inside its closed magma chamber. The chamber became over-pressurised by about 4,000–5,000 bar, with temperatures between 700 and 850 °C. The mountain started rumbling in 1812 and produced a dark cloud.

paragraphs.heading: The first blast
paragraphs.text: A giant eruption came on 5 April 1815. Thunderous detonation sounds followed, and people heard them 380 km away in Makassar on Sulawesi and 1,260 km away in Batavia, the city now called Jakarta, on Java. Volcanic ash started falling on East Java the next morning, 6 April. On 10 April a sound reached Trumon on Sumatra, more than 2,600 km away, and it was at first taken for gunfire.

paragraphs.heading: The night of 10 April
paragraphs.text: The eruptions grew stronger on 10 April, at about 7:00 in the evening. Three plumes rose and joined together. Around 8:00 pumice stones as wide as 20 cm began raining down, and ash followed between about 9:00 and 10:00. Soon afterwards a violent whirlwind struck Saugur, a village now called Sangar, and blew down nearly every house. Pyroclastic flows poured down to the sea on every side of the peninsula and wiped out the village of Tambora.

paragraphs.heading: Waves and a shorter mountain
paragraphs.text: On 10 April a tsunami of moderate size struck the coasts of various Indonesian islands, reaching as high as 4 m in Sanggar. Deaths linked to the tsunami have been estimated at around 4,600. Before the explosion the peak stood about 4,300 m high, among the tallest in the archipelago. The explosion cut its height by about one third, to 2,851 m.

paragraphs.heading: Ash around the world
paragraphs.text: The column from the eruption climbed into the stratosphere, higher than 43 km. The coarser ash settled out within one to two weeks. The finer ash stayed up for months or even a few years, at heights of 10–30 km. Winds carried these fine particles around the globe and created optical effects. In London, long and brilliantly coloured sunsets and twilights were a frequent sight from 28 June to 2 July 1815, and again from 3 September to 7 October of that year.
